acts.note.136:0.desc: Jesus began his public work at the height of interest in John's preaching, when the Jews were eagerly looking for the Messiah. John was an eager and earnest worker, while Jesus was a calm and happy laborer. John's message was repentance; Jesus always followed repentance with the gospel, the good tidings of the kingdom.
acts.note.136:1.desc: The Jews pictured the deliverer as the servant of the Lord, the son of David, the Son of Man, or the Son of God, and expected a Messiah who, like Moses, would miraculously free them from Rome. Yet they had no concept of human and divine natures joined in one personality; that incarnation was revealed only in Jesus.
acts.note.136:2.desc: In A.D. 26, almost thirty-one and a half years old, Jesus was baptized by John following the example of devout Israelites, a baptism of consecration, not repentance. His indwelling Adjuster departed and returned as a Personalized Adjuster, declaring him a beloved Son. That day ended the purely human life of Jesus.
acts.note.136:2.diff: The Gospels say the Holy Spirit descended like a dove, whereas The Urantia Book explains it as the return of the Personalized Adjuster, a form seen only by Jesus, while the voice was heard also by John and Jesus' two brothers.
acts.note.136:3.desc: Before his baptism Jesus had met and defeated Caligastia on Mount Hermon. After it he spent forty days in the Perean hills planning his public work. There he met Gabriel and the Constellation Father of Edentia and was told that his sovereignty was already complete and the rest of his life was his to choose.
acts.note.136:3.diff: The Gospels say the Spirit led him into the wilderness to fast forty days and be tempted by the devil, whereas The Urantia Book places the real struggle on Mount Hermon before the baptism and calls the forty days a time of planning and decision, not fasting.
acts.note.136:4.desc: Jesus decided not to teach alongside John until John's work was done, and, following Immanuel's instructions, to leave no permanent writing. He neither fasted nor suffered temptation, and on the third day he resolved always to choose the Father's will. He lived in a rock cavern near the village of Beit Adis.
acts.note.136:5.desc: On the third day Jesus beheld the assembled celestial hosts of Nebadon, including twelve legions of seraphim. He resolved not to use them unless the Father's will was evident and gave their command to his Personalized Adjuster, who told him it could prevent acts involving space but not those involving time.
acts.note.136:6.desc: When hunger came on the third day, Jesus decided not to create food by his creator powers but to obtain it as an ordinary man. He resolved to use superhuman power for others but never for himself, and summed up the decision in the Scripture that man shall not live by bread alone.
acts.note.136:6.diff: The Gospels say the devil tempted him after forty days of fasting to turn stones into bread, whereas The Urantia Book makes it Jesus' own decision in the face of hunger on the third day, the adversary's challenge being a later portrayal.
acts.note.136:7.desc: Jesus decided to exercise normal human care over his personal safety but to refuse superhuman intervention even in mortal danger. Sitting at the edge of a precipice, he knew he could leap unharmed, yet he refused a display defying his Father's law of gravity, and he kept this decision throughout his life.
acts.note.136:7.diff: The Gospels say the devil set Jesus on the pinnacle of the temple and told him to throw himself down, whereas The Urantia Book portrays a decision Jesus reached alone at the edge of a rocky precipice in the hills.
acts.note.136:8.desc: Jesus decided not to use superhuman power, signs, or wonders to win people's attention and allegiance. He knew short cuts such as seeming to walk on air from the temple pinnacle at Passover, but refused to compromise with worldly wisdom or wealth, choosing to build the kingdom in the natural, patient way.
acts.note.136:8.diff: The Gospels say the devil showed him all the kingdoms of the world from a high mountain and offered them for his worship, whereas The Urantia Book describes Jesus' own decision about using his powers to attract followers.
acts.note.136:9.desc: Choosing how to establish the kingdom of God, Jesus rejected beginning it with miracles and displays of power or with political and temporal authority. He concluded that the Messianic passages his mother had taught him did not refer to him, and he resolved to return to Galilee, quietly proclaim the kingdom, and leave the details to the Father.
acts.note.136:10.desc: On the last day of his isolation, before going down to join John and his disciples, Jesus made his final decision. He pledged to his Personalized Adjuster that in all other matters, too, he would be subject to the Father's will, and he came down the mountain his face shining with the glory of spiritual victory and moral achievement.
acts.note.137:0.desc: Early on Saturday, February 23, A.D. 26, Jesus came down from the hills and rejoined John's company encamped at Pella. All that day he mingled with the multitude, and he ministered to a lad hurt in a fall, taking him safely to his parents in the nearby village of Pella.
acts.note.137:1.desc: That Sabbath Andrew, who accompanied Jesus with the injured boy, asked to follow him and became the first apostle. His brother Simon, after consulting John, became the second and was named Peter. That night James and John the sons of Zebedee, back from searching the hills, sought out Jesus and were accepted.
acts.note.137:1.diff: Matthew, Mark, and Luke show Jesus calling fishermen at work beside the Sea of Galilee, whereas The Urantia Book says Andrew, Simon, and then James and John joined him at John's camp near Pella.
acts.map19.head: From Pella by Nazareth to Cana and Bethsaida
acts.map19.1.head: From Pella to Nazareth
acts.map19.1.body: Sunday morning, February 24, A.D. 26, Jesus took leave of John the Baptist by the river near Pella. On the way to Galilee with his four disciple-apostles, on the roadside near the Jordan, he met Philip and Nathaniel. They crossed the Jordan and, going by Nain, reached Nazareth late that evening and remained overnight with Joseph in Jesus' boyhood home.
acts.map19.2.head: By Magdala to Capernaum
acts.map19.2.body: The next day he sent his apostles on to Cana (dashed), stopped at Magdala to see his brother Jude, and arrived in Capernaum Monday night, going directly to the home of Zebedee.
acts.map19.3.head: The wedding at Cana
acts.map19.3.body: On Tuesday they all journeyed over to Cana. By noon on Wednesday almost a thousand guests had arrived for the wedding feast of Naomi and Johab.
acts.map19.4.head: To Bethsaida
acts.map19.4.body: Very early the next morning he and his six apostles went directly to the home of Zebedee at Bethsaida. The following morning he went with Zebedee to the boatshop. On Sabbath, March 2, he made his first public appearance after his baptism, in the Capernaum synagogue.
acts.note.137:2.desc: On February 24 Jesus took leave of John near Pella, while Ezra rejected Jesus and led many disciples south to form a separate sect. On the way to Galilee Jesus told Philip of Bethsaida to follow him and accepted Nathaniel of Cana, whom Philip brought. They spent the night at Joseph's home in Nazareth.
acts.note.137:2.diff: The Gospel of John says Jesus foresaw Nathaniel under the fig tree and Nathaniel confessed him Son of God, whereas The Urantia Book has no such foreknowledge or confession; Philip fetches him from under a mulberry tree.
acts.note.137:3.desc: The next day Jesus sent his apostles ahead to a wedding at Cana, saw his brother Jude at Magdala, and reached Zebedee's house in Capernaum Monday night. Mary, the family, and the disciples, expecting Gabriel's promise to be fulfilled and Jesus to show Messianic power at Cana, set out for Cana on Tuesday.
acts.note.137:4.desc: Almost a thousand guests came on Wednesday to the wedding of Naomi and Johab, hoping for a wonder. Jesus declined Mary's plea to reveal himself, but when the wine ran out, he felt compassion for his weeping mother, and at his desire the water in six stone waterpots became wine. The Urantia Book calls it a case of time being annihilated.
acts.note.137:4.diff: The Gospel of John presents it as the first sign, Jesus ordering the jars filled to manifest his glory, whereas The Urantia Book says it happened at his desire without his intent, and Jesus himself was the most surprised.
acts.map20.head: Calling and Ordaining the Apostles — Bethsaida and the Sea of Galilee
acts.map20.1.head: From Cana to Bethsaida
acts.map20.1.body: February, A.D. 26: very early the morning after the wedding at Cana, Jesus and his six apostles went directly to the home of Zebedee at Bethsaida. Through the tarrying time of March, April, May, and June he held over one hundred sessions with them.
acts.map20.2.head: Sent two and two; Jesus to Nazareth
acts.map20.2.body: On Sunday, June 23, he sent the six forth by twos: James and John to Kheresa, Andrew and Peter to Capernaum, Philip and Nathaniel to Tarichea. Meantime Jesus went over to Nazareth to visit his family; after two weeks they returned to the home of Zebedee.
acts.map20.3.head: Matthew and Simon the Zealot called
acts.map20.3.body: At the toll house in Capernaum he called Matthew; after a noontide luncheon at Matthew's house they called Simon the Zealot. That evening Matthew gave a banquet.
acts.map20.4.head: By boat to Kheresa
acts.map20.4.body: On the morrow all nine went by boat over to Kheresa to call James and Judas, the twin sons of Alpheus.
acts.map20.5.head: By boat to Tarichea
acts.map20.5.body: The eleven went by boat over to Tarichea, where Thomas and Judas Iscariot met them at the fisher-boat landing and were received.
acts.map20.6.head: By boat back to Capernaum
acts.map20.6.body: After a further day and a night of rest they departed by boat for Capernaum. Zebedee and Salome had turned their large home over to Jesus and his twelve apostles.
acts.map20.7.head: The ordination of the twelve
acts.map20.7.body: Just before noon on Sunday, January 12, A.D. 27, he called the apostles together along the seashore and journeyed with them to the highlands north of Capernaum for their ordination, returning that evening to the home of Zebedee. The next Sabbath, on the same highland, he consecrated the twelve.
acts.note.137:5.desc: The morning after the wedding Jesus left with six apostles for Zebedee's home at Bethsaida, telling them not to speak of the wine. That evening the apostles failed to grasp his mission. After a sleepless night by the lake, Jesus decided not to deny outright that he was the Messiah and told them to wait until John's preaching ended.
acts.note.137:5.diff: The Gospel of John says Jesus went down to Capernaum with his mother, brothers, and disciples, whereas The Urantia Book says he left without taking leave of his family, going only with six apostles to Zebedee's house at Bethsaida.
acts.note.137:6.desc: Jesus' first public appearance after his baptism came in the Capernaum synagogue on the Sabbath, March 2, A.D. 26. Before a crowd expecting wonders he read from Isaiah and said only that by patience they would see the glory of God. That afternoon he taught the apostles from a boat and told them to return to their regular work and wait.
acts.note.137:7.desc: For four months, March to June, Jesus held over one hundred sessions with the six apostles and his brother James, while Mary nearly lost hope. He explained the Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes, Zealots, Herodians, and Samaritans, and said he would join none of these groups.
acts.note.137:8.desc: On hearing of John's arrest, Jesus did his last work at the carpenter bench on June 18, A.D. 26. On the Sabbath, June 22, in the Capernaum synagogue, he preached his first great sermon on the kingdom, declaring that it is not of this world, is already within them, and is entered by faith. About one third of the hearers believed.
acts.note.138:0.desc: After the sermon on the kingdom, Jesus called only the six apostles and disclosed his plans to visit the cities around the Sea of Galilee. His brothers James and Jude were hurt at being left out, and since Cana he had kept apart from his mother; this gap with his family lasted until after the resurrection. Only Ruth, the youngest, stayed loyal.
acts.note.138:1.desc: On June 23, A.D. 26, Jesus sent the six out two and two for personal work, forbidding them to baptize and advising against public preaching: James and John to Kheresa, Andrew and Peter to Capernaum, Philip and Nathaniel to Tarichea. He also told each to choose one new apostle, to make twelve.
acts.note.138:2.desc: On their first two-week mission the six discovered the value of personal contact and returned to present their nominees. By unanimous vote Matthew Levi, Thomas Didymus, James Alpheus, Judas Alpheus, Simon Zelotes, and Judas Iscariot were accepted, chosen respectively by Andrew, Philip, James, John, Peter, and Nathaniel.
acts.note.138:3.desc: The next day Jesus told Matthew at the Capernaum toll house, "Follow me," and after lunch he called Simon Zelotes, Peter's nominee. That evening at Matthew's banquet, Pharisees objected that Jesus ate with publicans and sinners, and he answered that he had come to call not the righteous but sinners.
acts.note.138:3.diff: The Gospels show Jesus calling Matthew as he passed the tax office, whereas The Urantia Book says he visited a prepared Matthew after Andrew's nomination and the vote, and called Simon Zelotes the same day.
acts.note.138:4.desc: The next day the nine crossed by boat to Kheresa and called James and Judas, the twin sons of Alpheus, nominated by James and John Zebedee. Jesus taught them never to refuse to eat with Pharisees, sinners, publicans, or Romans, and that night he first taught about the origin, nature, and destiny of unclean spirits.
acts.note.138:5.desc: At Tarichea Jesus accepted Thomas, Philip's nominee, though he lacked faith, and Judas Iscariot, Nathaniel's nominee. After instructing the twelve about the Holy Spirit and the ministry of seraphim, he went to Capernaum to stay in the house Zebedee had turned over to them. That evening Judas asked why Jesus did not free John.
acts.note.138:6.desc: The following week the six new apostles were trained intensively by their nominators. Jesus set Wednesday as a weekly day of rest and urged them not to build legends or a cult around him but to proclaim the gospel of the kingdom and the revelation of the Father. He planned months of quiet work around the Sea of Galilee.
acts.note.138:7.desc: Early on the first Sunday, Peter, James Zebedee, and Judas Iscariot asked what places they would hold in the kingdom, and Jesus rebuked them, saying his kingdom is not of this world. The apostles pledged their loyalty. Finding funds short, Jesus had them alternate two weeks of fishing with two weeks of personal work, a plan followed to the end of A.D. 26.
acts.note.138:8.desc: In mid-August, A.D. 26, the twelve went out two and two to fields Andrew assigned, Jesus joining each pair in turn. He taught forgiveness of sin through faith and told them not to discuss John's imprisonment, the voice at the baptism, or the wine at Cana. He also taught that women are equal with men in the kingdom of heaven.
acts.note.138:9.desc: The five months of alternating fishing and personal work were a grueling test for the twelve, but they stayed loyal and came to feel Jesus was their closest friend. Meanwhile his family, except Ruth, practically deserted him. The apostles worked in Capernaum, Chorazin, Magdala, Cana, and elsewhere, and arranged for their families' support.
acts.note.138:10.desc: The twelve organized themselves: Andrew as chairman; Peter, James, and John as Jesus' personal companions; Philip as steward; Nathaniel caring for the families; Matthew as fiscal agent; Thomas managing the itinerary; the Alpheus twins managing the multitudes; Simon Zelotes in charge of recreation; Judas as treasurer. On January 12, A.D. 27, Jesus formally ordained them ambassadors of the kingdom.
acts.intro.139: The choosing of the twelve apostles
acts.note.139:0.desc: Though Jesus repeatedly dashed his apostles' hopes of personal exaltation, only one deserted him, a testimony to the charm of his life. The twelve represented many types of temperament, and all but the Alpheus twins were graduates of the synagogue schools. Calling them "ignorant and unlearned" meant they were untrained in rabbinic lore and methods of interpretation.
acts.note.139:0.diff: The Gospels say Jesus appointed the twelve together on a mountain, whereas The Urantia Book says he first called six, each of whom then nominated one more to make twelve. It also notes that the Alpheus twins were called Thaddeus and Lebbeus.
acts.note.139:1.desc: Andrew, born in Capernaum as the eldest of five children, was an unmarried fisherman of thirty-three in A.D. 26. Chairman of the twelve, he was a good organizer, a better administrator, and the best judge of men. He lived without jealousy of his brother Peter and was finally crucified at Patrae in Achaia.
acts.note.139:2.desc: Simon Peter, a married fisherman of Bethsaida, joined at thirty. Impulsive, optimistic, and eloquent, he was a natural leader who most admired Jesus' supernal tenderness. A strange mixture of courage and cowardice, he denied the Master when ridiculed. The greatest preacher of the twelve, he was crucified in Rome.
acts.note.139:3.desc: James Zebedee, a fisherman and father of four, joined at thirty; with his brother John he was nicknamed "sons of thunder." His weaknesses were a fiery temper and unexplained silences, but he was a well-balanced thinker who could see all sides of a question. He was the first apostle to die, put to the sword by Herod Agrippa.
acts.note.139:4.desc: John Zebedee, at twenty-four the youngest apostle, served as Jesus' personal agent in family affairs. Conceit was his weakness, but he was dependable and daring, following Jesus to the end on the night of his arrest. He became the apostle of love, wrote the Book of Revelation on Patmos, and died a natural death at Ephesus in A.D. 103.
acts.note.139:5.desc: Philip of Bethsaida, the fifth apostle chosen, was twenty-seven and recently married. Lacking imagination but methodical and reliable, he served as steward of the apostolic group and was a persuasive personal worker whose method was "Come and see." He had great success in Samaria and was crucified and buried at Hierapolis.
acts.note.139:6.desc: Nathaniel, the sixth apostle, brought by Philip, was twenty-five, unmarried, and the support of his aged parents at Cana. Honest and without guile, though given to pride and prejudice, he was the group's philosopher and storyteller who eased tensions with humor. He looked after the apostles' families and died in India.
acts.note.139:7.desc: Matthew Levi, the seventh apostle, chosen by Andrew, was a thirty-one-year-old customs collector of Capernaum. As fiscal agent he raised the group's funds and secretly gave almost all his own wealth to the work, known only to Jesus. His notes became the basis of the Gospel according to Matthew, and he was put to death at Lysimachia in Thrace.
acts.note.139:8.desc: Thomas Didymus, the eighth apostle, chosen by Philip, was a twenty-nine-year-old fisherman of Tarichea, formerly a carpenter and stone mason. His analytical, skeptical mind made him doubt, yet he was honest and courageous, and once a decision was made he was first to say "Let's go!" He revered Jesus' balanced character and was put to death in Malta.
acts.note.139:9.desc: James and Judas, the twin sons of Alpheus, were twenty-six-year-old fishermen near Kheresa, chosen by James and John Zebedee. Commonplace men with neither strong nor weak points, they managed the multitudes and did odd jobs, greatly encouraging the common people. Loyal to the end, they returned to their families and nets after the crucifixion.
acts.note.139:11.desc: Simon Zelotes, the eleventh apostle, chosen by Peter, was a twenty-eight-year-old Capernaum merchant and ardent patriot of the Zealots. He organized the group's recreation and excelled at leading waverers into faith, but never fully shed his nationalism. After the persecutions he went to Africa, where he died.
acts.note.139:12.desc: Judas Iscariot, the twelfth apostle, chosen by Nathaniel, was born in Kerioth, the only Judean of the twelve, unmarried, and thirty. An able treasurer, he was a spoiled child who overrated his own importance and nursed grudges. After Jesus publicly overruled his protest over the broken box of incense, he betrayed Jesus in revenge and finally took his own life.
acts.note.140:0.desc: Just before noon on Sunday, January 12, A.D. 27, Jesus walked along the seashore calling the twelve, first Andrew and Peter, then James and John, then the others two by two. He led them up to the highlands north of Capernaum and began instructing them in preparation for their formal ordination.
acts.note.140:1.desc: Before the ordination Jesus taught the seated twelve that the Father's kingdom is an everlasting rule set up in the hearts of men, its power lying not in armies or riches. They enter its door by faith but must bear the fruits of the spirit, and whoever would be great must become a minister to all.
acts.note.140:2.desc: Jesus had the twelve kneel in a circle about him and placed his hands on the head of each, beginning with Judas Iscariot and ending with Andrew. Then he prayed, commending them to the Father, and the apostles silently came forward one by one to embrace him.
acts.note.140:3.desc: Right after the ordination Jesus charged his new ambassadors: happy are the poor in spirit, the meek, and others; they are the salt of the earth and the light of the world; they must love their enemies, not judge others, and know false prophets by their fruits. At sundown they came down the mountain asking no questions.
acts.note.140:3.diff: The Gospel of Matthew (chapters 5–7) presents this as the Sermon on the Mount heard by astonished crowds, whereas The Urantia Book makes it an ordination charge to the twelve alone, without sayings like the jot and tittle, the narrow gate, or the house on the rock.
acts.note.140:4.desc: The Urantia Book explains that the so-called Sermon on the Mount is not the gospel of Jesus but his ordination charge to the twelve. Salt was precious, even used for money; light should not draw attention to itself; strong character comes from actually doing right; and moral character can grow.
acts.note.140:4.diff: The Gospels give only the sayings about salt and light, whereas The Urantia Book adds the background that salt was used as money and a lengthy commentary on light, character, and happiness.
acts.note.140:5.desc: Jesus teaches fatherly love, loving others as he loves them, beyond brotherly love that loves the neighbor as oneself. The first four beatitudes are faith attitudes; the last four (mourning, mercy, peacemaking, persecution) are supreme reactions of fatherly love. The beatitudes rest on faith and love, not law.
acts.note.140:5.diff: The Gospels list the beatitudes in a single series, whereas The Urantia Book divides them into four faith attitudes and four reactions of fatherly love and arranges them in a different order.
acts.note.140:6.desc: On the evening of the ordination, in Zebedee's garden, Jesus taught the apostles further at Andrew's request. He said he came not to destroy the law and the prophets but to fulfill them, answered several apostles' questions, and then held private talks with each until dawn, not waking the sleeping twins.
acts.note.140:6.diff: The Gospels present these sayings as part of one sermon on the mount, whereas The Urantia Book places them that evening in Zebedee's garden as answers to the apostles' questions.
acts.sub.140:6.3–13: The new commandments — "You have heard … but I say"
acts.note.sub:140:6.3–13.desc: When Peter asked for a new commandment, Jesus looked beyond the commandments against killing and adultery to motive and intent. Answering James on divorce, Nathaniel on "an eye for an eye," and Thomas on holding all in common, he taught secret good deeds and prayer, treasure in heaven, and freedom from anxiety about tomorrow.
acts.note.sub:140:6.3–13.diff: Matthew forbids divorce except for unchastity and includes the ban on oaths and the Lord's Prayer, whereas in The Urantia Book Jesus refuses to legislate on divorce, and oaths and the Lord's Prayer are not mentioned here.
acts.note.140:7.desc: The next day, when Thomas asked to stay a few days longer, Jesus agreed to remain until the Sabbath. That week the twelve taught visitors who had come to Bethsaida from Tyre, Sidon, Damascus, Jerusalem, and elsewhere, and Jesus repeatedly stated the two motives of his mission: to reveal the Father and to make men son-conscious.
acts.note.140:8.desc: On Thursday afternoon Jesus took Peter, James, and John out on the lake and talked about the kingdom for four hours. He covered doing the Father's will and his political, social, and economic attitudes and personal religion, teaching nonresistance and no retaliation, avoidance of political issues, the importance of the family, and the influence of wealth on men.
acts.note.140:9.desc: The next Sabbath Jesus took the apostles back to the highland of their ordination for the consecration of the twelve. Calling each before him, he commissioned them to go into all the world and preach the glad tidings of the kingdom, sending them as sheep among wolves, wise as serpents and harmless as doves. No new teaching was given.
acts.note.140:10.desc: That rainy evening, indoors, Jesus taught the twelve what they must be, not what they must do. He told Thomas that becoming as little children means the relation of a child to the Father, answered Simon Zelotes that all men are the sons of God, and told John the three essentials of the kingdom of heaven.
acts.map21.head: Along the Jordan Valley to Judea
acts.map21.1.head: From Bethsaida to Tarichea
acts.map21.1.body: On January 19, A.D. 27, Jesus and the twelve left Zebedee's house near noon, going up to Jerusalem for the Passover by way of the Jordan valley. The first day they journeyed only as far as Tarichea, where they rested for the night.
acts.map21.2.head: The Jordan near Pella
acts.map21.2.body: Where John had preached about one year before and where Jesus had received baptism. They tarried more than two weeks, and several hundred people came from Galilee, Phoenicia, Syria, the Decapolis, Perea, and Judea.
acts.map21.3.head: Near Amathus
acts.map21.3.body: They remained almost three weeks. The apostles preached twice daily, and Jesus preached each Sabbath afternoon. Teherma, a Persian doing business at Damascus, came to see him.
acts.map21.4.head: Bethany beyond Jordan
acts.map21.4.body: On February 26 they journeyed down the Jordan to the ford near Bethany in Perea, where John first made proclamation of the coming kingdom, and remained there four weeks.
acts.map21.5.head: Three days in the hills
acts.map21.5.body: In the second week Jesus took Peter, James, and John into the hills across the river and south of Jericho for a three days' rest, teaching them.
acts.map21.6.head: The apostles' visits to Jericho
acts.map21.6.body: Several times each week Andrew assigned apostolic couples to go up to Jericho for a day or two. There the commission to minister to the afflicted was first fully carried into effect (dotted).
acts.map21.7.head: By Jericho to Bethany
acts.map21.7.body: On the way up to Jerusalem they stopped in Jericho, where Jesus spent three days with a delegation from Mesopotamia. On Monday, the last day of March, they went up the hills and rested five days in the home of Lazarus at Bethany.
acts.note.141:0.desc: On Sunday, January 19, A.D. 27, Jesus and the twelve prepared to leave their Bethsaida headquarters to go up to Jerusalem for the Passover. Just before they left, Andrew found Jesus weeping in a boat down the beach, because none of his father Joseph's family had come to bid them Godspeed.
acts.note.141:1.desc: To avoid Herod's notice, Jesus went south with his apostles, stopping the first night at Tarichea and then staying over two weeks at the place on the Jordan near Pella where he had been baptized. Jesus did no public preaching, and the apostles taught John's disciples without baptizing.
acts.note.141:2.desc: The night before leaving Pella, Jesus taught that the kingdom of heaven is not the rule of a Messiah on David's throne but the realization and acknowledgment of God's rule in human hearts. When the Father's will is your law, you are hardly in the kingdom; when it becomes your will, you are truly in it.
acts.note.141:3.desc: Jesus and the apostles stayed near Amathus for almost three weeks; the apostles preached twice daily, and Jesus preached each Sabbath afternoon. Andrew handled the frictions between John's disciples and the new ones, while Jesus stayed out of them. The chapter portrays Jesus' strong and manly personality.
acts.note.141:4.desc: At Amathus Jesus taught a new concept of God: a Father who loves each person, not a great bookkeeper recording sins. He sought to free the apostles from the idea of animal sacrifice and taught them to minister to the sick by distinguishing three afflictions: diseases of the flesh, troubled minds, and possession by evil spirits.
acts.note.141:5.desc: When James Zebedee asked how they might all learn to see alike, Jesus answered that he had never taught them to see alike. What he asked was spiritual unity, springing from a common motive of doing the Father's will and a common goal of finding the Father and becoming like him.
acts.note.141:6.desc: In the last week at Amathus, Simon Zelotes brought Teherma, a Persian trader of Damascus, to Jesus. When Simon failed to persuade him, Jesus taught him not to try to take error out of seekers' hearts but to feed their hungry souls, and Teherma entered the kingdom. That night Jesus spoke on the new life in the kingdom.
acts.note.141:7.desc: On February 26 Jesus and his company went to the ford near Bethany in Perea, where John had first proclaimed the kingdom, and taught there for four weeks. In the second week Jesus rested three days with Peter, James, and John in the hills south of Jericho, teaching them new truths such as revealing God as Father and salvation by faith.
acts.note.141:7.diff: The Gospel of John says Jesus baptized in Judea while John was not yet imprisoned, whereas The Urantia Book says John was already in prison and the apostles did not baptize at this time.
acts.note.141:8.desc: During the four weeks at Bethany beyond Jordan, Andrew sent apostolic couples up to Jericho, where they went from house to house ministering to the afflicted. There the commission to preach the glad tidings and minister to the sick was first fully carried out. On the way to Jerusalem Jesus spent three days with a delegation from Mesopotamia.
acts.map22.head: First Work with the Apostles — Judea, Samaria, and the Decapolis
acts.map22.1.head: Bethany and Jerusalem
acts.map22.1.body: At the end of March, A.D. 27, they rested five days at the home of Lazarus in Bethany, and on Sunday, April 6, went down to Jerusalem. Through April they worked in Jerusalem, going out each evening to spend the night at Bethany.
acts.map22.2.head: Bethlehem and Hebron
acts.map22.2.body: By the end of April the opposition had grown, and they went south to Bethlehem and Hebron, spending all of May in house-to-house visitation. Meanwhile Jesus and Abner visited the Nazarite colony at Engedi (dashed).
acts.map22.3.head: The tents at Gethsemane
acts.map22.3.body: Returning in the first days of June, they lived the whole month in tents in the park known as Gethsemane, on the western slope of the Mount of Olives. Sabbath weekends they usually spent at Bethany.
acts.map22.4.head: Bethel, Arimathea, and Thamna
acts.map22.4.body: At the end of June they went north into Samaria and tarried over the Sabbath at Bethel. Invited by citizens of Arimathea and Thamna, they spent more than two weeks teaching in this region.
acts.map22.5.head: Archelais and Phasaelis
acts.map22.5.body: The first half of August they made headquarters at these Greek cities near the Jordan, their first experience preaching to well-nigh exclusive gatherings of gentiles.
acts.map22.6.head: Sychar and Mount Gerizim
acts.map22.6.body: About the middle of the month they set out for Sychar. At Jacob's well Jesus talked with Nalda, a Samaritan woman; they camped on Mount Gerizim until the end of August.
acts.map22.7.head: The camp on the slopes of Mount Gilboa
acts.map22.7.body: September and October were spent in retirement at this secluded camp, teaching the apostles. In October came a three weeks' conference with the apostles of John.
acts.map22.8.head: The Greek cities of the Decapolis
acts.map22.8.body: In November and December they worked quietly, chiefly in Scythopolis, Gerasa, Abila, and Gadara. The text does not give the order of the cities or the roads between them.
acts.map22.9.head: By Pella to Capernaum
acts.map22.9.body: Late in December they taught again near the Jordan, close by Pella. In January, A.D. 28, they heard of John's execution; on January 13 they arrived in Capernaum and made their headquarters at the home of Zebedee in Bethsaida.
acts.note.141:9.desc: On Monday, the last day of March, Jesus and the apostles climbed toward Jerusalem and rested five days at the home of Lazarus in Bethany, which became their headquarters during the Jerusalem stay. On Sunday morning, April 6, Jesus and the twelve went to Jerusalem together for the first time.
acts.note.142:0.desc: Through April Jesus and the apostles worked in Jerusalem and spent nights at Bethany, Jesus sometimes staying at the home of Flavius, a Greek Jew. On the first day he called on his old friend Annas, the former high priest, but was received coldly, and after a word about fear and pride he took his leave.
acts.note.142:1.desc: Throughout the month Jesus or one of the apostles taught daily in the temple. Their message was that the kingdom is at hand, that it is entered by faith in the fatherhood of God, that love is the rule of living, and that obedience to the Father's will is its law. Through the Passover crowds the gospel began spreading across the empire and the East.
acts.note.142:2.desc: Jacob, a wealthy Jewish trader from Crete, met Jesus secretly at Flavius's home and asked how the wrathful Yahweh fit with a loving Father. Jesus said the Father is changeless but man's concept of him has grown, illustrating with a father's discipline of his children. Jacob, a father of six, believed.
acts.note.142:3.desc: That night Jesus taught the apostles how Israel's concept of God grew from Yahweh through the Most High, El Shaddai, Elohim, and the Supreme Yahweh to the Father in heaven. He also explained that the old ten commandments before Sinai gave way to Moses' new ones and then to the law of loving God and neighbor.
acts.note.142:4.desc: Flavius, a Greek Jew, feared his collection of images would offend Jesus, but Jesus took interest in every piece and approved of appreciating beauty. He explained that Moses' ban on images was for its own time. Flavius believed and was baptized by John's disciples.
acts.note.142:5.desc: During Passover week in the temple, a man from Damascus asked how they could know that Jesus was sent by God and that they could enter the kingdom. Jesus answered that, as no worthy father leaves his children in anxiety, the heavenly Father leaves no child of faith in doubt, and that loving one another is evidence of being born of the spirit.
acts.note.142:6.desc: Nicodemus, a wealthy and elderly member of the Sanhedrin, arranged through Andrew to visit Jesus one evening at Flavius's home. Jesus told him that a man must be born from above, of the spirit, to enter the kingdom, and that the Father's spirit already dwelt within him. Nicodemus was deeply impressed but went away bewildered.
acts.note.142:6.diff: The Gospel of John has Nicodemus come by night because of Jesus' signs and hear of birth by water and Spirit, the serpent, and the only Son, whereas The Urantia Book bases his coming on Jesus' teaching, omits those sayings, and sets the meeting at Flavius's home.
acts.note.142:7.desc: On the Wednesday after Passover week, at Bethany, Thomas asked how people of the kingdom should live. All afternoon and evening Jesus used the family to illustrate the relation between God and man, naming seven features of true family life, and warned against literally applying spiritual teachings to material problems like slavery, poverty, and property.
acts.note.142:8.desc: As opposition grew in late April, Jesus and the apostles spent May doing house-to-house work in Bethlehem and Hebron, while Jesus and Abner visited the Nazarite colony at Engedi. In June they camped at Gethsemane, but when Simon of the Sanhedrin publicly espoused Jesus' teachings, a new agitation for his arrest arose, and he decided to retire to Samaria and the Decapolis.
acts.note.143:0.desc: At the end of June, A.D. 27, Jesus and the twelve left their tents and belongings at Lazarus's home in Bethany and went north into Samaria. They spent the Sabbath at Bethel and taught people from Gophna, Ephraim, Arimathea, and Thamna for over two weeks. The apostles overcame much of their prejudice against Samaritans, but Judas Iscariot did not.
acts.note.143:1.desc: In the first half of August the apostolic party preached for the first time to almost wholly gentile audiences in the Greek cities of Archelais and Phasaelis. When Philip reported that the gentiles called the gospel fit only for weaklings and slaves, Jesus gave an impassioned address on the supreme spiritual courage that kingdom service demands, and the apostles' preaching became bold.
acts.note.143:2.desc: One evening Andrew asked how John's teaching of self-denial differed from Jesus' self-control. Jesus answered that John's way was a religion of self-examination and self-denial, but he brought a new message of self-forgetfulness and self-mastery. Those born of the spirit gain, by faith, the liberty of self-mastery.
acts.note.143:3.desc: When tension rose among the apostles and Andrew asked for help, Jesus did not intervene but invited them to rest three days on Mount Sartaba. They rested without discussing their troubles, and on coming down found that many problems had resolved themselves; relations with John's followers improved too. In mid-month Jesus set out for Sychar.
acts.note.143:4.desc: Enmity between Jews and Samaritans began about 700 B.C., when Sargon, king of Assyria, carried away people of the northern kingdom and settled other peoples there. It deepened when Samaritans hindered the rebuilding of Jerusalem after the exile and when their temple on Mount Gerizim was built and destroyed. Going to Samaria tested the apostles' loyalty.
acts.note.143:5.desc: About six o'clock on a summer evening at Jacob's well, Jesus asked Nalda of Sychar for a drink and spoke of living water. Sobered by his command to bring her husband, she asked where to worship; Jesus spoke of worship in spirit and truth and first openly declared, "I who speak to you am he." Nalda left her pitcher and ran to the city.
acts.note.143:5.diff: The Gospel of John says Jesus told her she had had five husbands, whereas The Urantia Book says he never said this; she had lived with four men after her husband cast her aside. Where John says Messiah, Nalda speaks of the Converter John had preached.
acts.note.143:6.desc: When Nalda brought out the crowd, Jesus told the apostles urging him to eat that his food was to do the will of him who sent him, and that the fields were white for the harvest. After preaching two days in Sychar, they camped on Mount Gerizim and until the end of August proclaimed the fatherhood of God in the Samaritan cities.
acts.note.143:6.diff: The Gospel of John closes with many Samaritans believing in Jesus as Savior of the world, whereas The Urantia Book adds that the apostles did not yet baptize those who asked and that the group stayed on Mount Gerizim until late August.
acts.note.143:7.desc: At the evening conferences on Mount Gerizim, Jesus teaches that true religion is the individual soul's relation with the Creator, while organized religion is an attempt to socialize worship. Worship must alternate with service, and work with play. Prayer is self-reminding, sublime thinking; worship is self-forgetting, superthinking.
acts.note.144:0.desc: In September and October Jesus and the apostles withdrew to a secluded camp on the slopes of Mount Gilboa, on the borders of Samaria and the Decapolis. The reasons were the hostility of the Jerusalem rulers, the suspicions of Herod Antipas, who still held John, and tensions with John's disciples; Jesus wished his public launch not to embarrass John.
acts.note.144:1.desc: On Gilboa Jesus gave three reasons for their retirement and told the twelve of his early life, his experience on Mount Hermon, and part of the forty days after his baptism, charging them to tell no one until he had returned to the Father. The apostles disagreed over whether the kingdom had come. Prayer and worship were September's theme, and Thomas asked to be taught to pray.
acts.note.144:2.desc: One afternoon in the third week on Gilboa, Jesus recalled the prayer John had taught and said prayer is the spontaneous expression of the soul's attitude toward the spirit, the breath of the soul. He urged persistent prayer with the friend borrowing three loaves at midnight, the ask, seek, and knock sayings, and the father who gives no stone for bread.
acts.note.144:2.diff: The Gospel of Luke has Jesus give the Lord's Prayer as soon as a disciple asks, then the parables, whereas The Urantia Book has him answer Thomas with a discourse first and give the prayer later; a watersnake replaces the egg and scorpion.
acts.sub.144:2.5: The story of the unjust judge and the poor widow
acts.note.sub:144:2.5.desc: Jesus told of a judge who neither feared God nor regarded man, who at last avenged a needy widow because she kept coming to trouble him. He added that this encourages persistence in prayer, not the idea that petitions change the Father.
acts.note.sub:144:2.5.diff: The Gospel of Luke ends with God speedily avenging his elect, whereas The Urantia Book says persistence does not change the Father but changes one's attitude and enlarges the soul's capacity to receive the spirit.
acts.note.144:3.desc: When James Zebedee asked for a form of prayer for new believers, Jesus gave the prayer he had taught his brothers and sisters in Nazareth. He always taught them to pray in secret and said effective prayer must be unselfish, believing, sincere, intelligent, and trustful in the Father's will.
acts.note.144:3.diff: The Lord's Prayer in the Gospels asks for daily bread, whereas the prayer in The Urantia Book asks for bread for tomorrow and the water of life and ends by asking to be made perfect; the kingdom, power, and glory line was a later addition.
acts.note.144:4.desc: In the days after the discourse on prayer, Jesus taught more about prayer and worship. Earnest prayer expands the soul's capacity for spiritual receptivity, sonship is a gift of grace, and prayer is an antidote for harmful introspection. The Master usually prayed in the plural and very rarely prayed aloud.
acts.note.144:5.desc: During his earth life Jesus introduced the apostles to various forms of prayer as illustrations of other matters, forbidding them to teach these to the multitudes. Many came from other inhabited planets, though Jesus did not reveal this. Specific permission was granted to transcribe seven specimen prayers into this record.
acts.note.144:6.desc: In early October a chance market meeting between Philip's group and John's apostles led to a three-week joint conference of twenty-four men at the Gilboa camp. Jesus was absent for two weeks after the first. They agreed to adopt the new prayer and that while John lived only his apostles would baptize. The camp broke up on November 2.
acts.note.144:7.desc: In November and December Jesus and the twenty-four worked quietly in the Greek cities of the Decapolis, chiefly Scythopolis, Gerasa, Abila, and Gadara. They worked in pairs, one of Jesus' apostles with one of John's, one teaching and the other baptizing, and John's followers gave up nearly everything but water baptism to join the work.
acts.note.144:8.desc: In late December the group moved near the Jordan close to Pella and again taught and preached. One afternoon John's friends brought the last question from John, who had been in prison a year and a half. Many who heard Jesus that day received John's baptism, and the followers of John and Jesus became truly united.
acts.note.144:8.diff: The Gospels go on to Jesus' rebuke of Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum, whereas The Urantia Book has no such rebuke here and says that this event truly united the followers of John and Jesus.
acts.note.sub:144:8.2–8.desc: John's friends asked Jesus whether he was truly the Deliverer or they should look for another. Jesus told them to tell John he was not forgotten and that the poor have good tidings preached to them. To the crowd he praised John as more than a prophet and likened this generation to children in the market place. The messengers went to Machaerus to tell John.
acts.note.sub:144:8.2–8.diff: The Gospels have Jesus answer by listing miracles such as the blind seeing and the dead raised, whereas The Urantia Book mentions only good tidings preached to the poor, and Jesus does not call John Elijah.
acts.note.144:9.desc: John the Baptist was executed by order of Herod Antipas on the evening of January 10, A.D. 28. His disciples obtained his body, later burying it at Sebaste, Abner's home, and brought the news to the camp near Pella. Jesus said the time had come to proclaim the kingdom openly and left for Capernaum on the morning of January 13.
acts.note.144:9.diff: The Gospels tell of Herodias's daughter dancing at Herod's birthday feast and asking for John's head, whereas The Urantia Book here records only the date, the execution, and the burial at Sebaste.
acts.intro.145: The beginning of the Galilean work
acts.map23.head: The First Public Preaching Tour of Galilee
acts.map23.1.head: Capernaum and Bethsaida
acts.map23.1.body: Arriving in Capernaum the evening of Tuesday, January 13, A.D. 28, they made their headquarters at the home of Zebedee in Bethsaida. Jesus taught the multitude from a boat by the seaside; after sunset on the Sabbath the sick crowded to the Zebedee home.
acts.map23.2.head: Rimmon
acts.map23.2.body: On the afternoon of Sunday, January 18, the first public preaching tour began. At Rimmon they made plain the difference between the older Babylonian and Zoroastrian beliefs and the new gospel.
acts.map23.3.head: Jotapata
acts.map23.3.body: The common people heard them gladly. On the second evening Jesus spoke on prayer, thanksgiving, and worship.
acts.map23.4.head: Ramah
acts.map23.4.body: The discussion with the aged Greek philosopher on science, philosophy, and religion.
acts.map23.5.head: Zebulun and Iron
acts.map23.5.body: By Zebulun, in the order of the text's list, to Iron. At Iron he cleansed the leper; thronged by the sick, he rose early the next day and left the village.
acts.map23.6.head: Gischala and Chorazin
acts.map23.6.body: Two days at Gischala, then almost a week at Chorazin, where they were unable to win many believers.
acts.map23.7.head: Through Capernaum to Madon
acts.map23.7.body: Passing quietly through Capernaum, they went on to the village of Madon, where they fared little better.
acts.map23.8.head: Cana
acts.map23.8.body: A sympathetic hearing. Titus, a prominent citizen of Capernaum, came and besought Jesus to heal his son.
acts.map23.9.head: Nain
acts.map23.9.body: Near the gate of the city they met the funeral procession of a widow's only son. Jesus said the boy was not dead, but the report went abroad that he had been raised.
acts.map23.10.head: Endor
acts.map23.10.body: Escaping the multitudes for a few days, Jesus told the story of King Saul and the witch of Endor.
acts.map23.11.head: Back to Capernaum
acts.map23.11.body: Arriving in Capernaum on Wednesday, March 17, they spent two weeks at the Bethsaida headquarters.
acts.note.145:0.desc: Jesus and the apostles reached Capernaum on Tuesday evening, January 13, and made Zebedee's house in Bethsaida their headquarters. From Wednesday to Friday Jesus instructed the apostles for their first public preaching tour. Late Friday evening his baby sister Ruth secretly visited him, and they spent almost an hour together in a boat.
acts.note.145:0.diff: The Gospels say Jesus went to Galilee to preach when he heard John was arrested, whereas The Urantia Book says he prepared his first public tour only after John's execution, and it adds Ruth's visit.
acts.note.145:1.desc: On Friday morning, crowded at the seaside, Jesus got into the boat "Simon," Peter's former fishing vessel, and taught for over two hours. He then told David Zebedee and his associates, who had caught nothing all night, to let down their nets in the deep; they caught enough fish to nearly sink three boats, and they left their nets to follow Jesus.
acts.note.145:1.diff: The Gospel of Luke presents a miracle from Simon Peter's boat leading to the calling of Peter, James, and John, whereas The Urantia Book says it involved David Zebedee and his associates and was no miracle: Jesus, knowing the fishes' habits, simply directed them to a school.
acts.note.145:2.desc: The next Sabbath afternoon, in the Capernaum synagogue, Jesus read from Exodus and Isaiah and preached on the will of the Father in heaven, teaching a personal religion in which God loves each individual, not a national religion. Afterward he roused a young man seized by epilepsy and visited Peter's sick mother-in-law to comfort her.
acts.note.145:2.diff: The Gospels say only that people were astonished at the authority of his teaching, whereas The Urantia Book gives the sermon in detail, citing Jeremiah and Ezekiel on personal religion.
acts.sub.145:2.12–14: The epileptic youth healed in the synagogue
acts.note.sub:145:2.12–14.desc: As Jesus finished speaking, a young man in the congregation had a violent epileptic seizure and cried out that Jesus was the holy one of God. Jesus quieted the people, took his hand, and told him to come out of it, and he soon awoke. People thought an evil spirit had been cast out, and the report spread through Capernaum.
acts.note.sub:145:2.12–14.diff: The Gospels say an unclean spirit convulsed the man and came out, whereas The Urantia Book says he was not possessed but an epileptic, was not healed then, and was actually cured only after sundown.
acts.sub.145:2.15–16: The fever of Amatha, Peter's mother-in-law
acts.note.sub:145:2.15–16.desc: On the way back from the synagogue, Jesus visited Amatha, Peter's mother-in-law, who had had chills and fever for days. He took her hand and stroked her brow to comfort her, and just then her fever broke. Some apostles took it for another miracle and hurried out to spread the news.
acts.note.sub:145:2.15–16.diff: The Gospels say the fever left her when Jesus took her hand and she rose and served them, whereas The Urantia Book says her malarial fever happened to subside, and her real cure came after sundown in the front-yard event.
acts.note.145:3.desc: When the Sabbath ended at sundown, almost a thousand sick people and their families thronged the front yard of Zebedee's home in Bethsaida. As Jesus said that, if it were the Father's will, he desired to see his children made whole, 683 men, women, and children were healed. Jesus was the most surprised, and such a mass healing never occurred again.
acts.note.145:3.diff: The Gospels say Jesus healed the sick and cast out demons, whereas The Urantia Book says the healing of 683 was unintended: the Personalized Adjuster ruled on Jesus' expressed desire, and Jesus himself was the most surprised.
acts.note.145:4.desc: That evening the apostles were wildly elated, thinking the kingdom had come with power, but Jesus was nowhere to be found. Returning late, he refused their congratulations and told them to rejoice more in power to save souls than in healing bodies. The disappointed and perplexed apostles went to bed.
acts.note.145:5.desc: Before dawn on Sunday Jesus went out alone to pray, seeking wisdom so that physical healing would not overshadow his spiritual ministry. Peter, James, and John, and then Andrew, came urging him back to the crowds, but he refused, and on the afternoon of January 18, A.D. 28, he set out on his first public preaching tour of Galilee.
acts.intro.146: Setting out on the first preaching tour
acts.note.146:0.desc: The first public preaching tour of Galilee began on Sunday, January 18, A.D. 28, and lasted about two months, until the return to Capernaum on March 17. Jesus and the twelve, assisted by John's former apostles, preached and baptized believers in Rimmon, Jotapata, Ramah, Iron, Cana, Nain, Endor, and other towns.
acts.note.146:0.diff: The Gospels summarize Jesus preaching in synagogues throughout Galilee, healing and casting out demons, whereas The Urantia Book names the towns and dates and says the apostles were for the first time allowed to preach and baptize without restraint.
acts.note.146:1.desc: At Rimmon, once dedicated to the Babylonian air god Ramman, Jesus and the twenty-four spent much time explaining how the gospel differed from older Babylonian and Zoroastrian beliefs. Peter preached on Aaron and the golden calf, and Todan first heard the gospel here, later carrying it beyond Mesopotamia.
acts.note.146:2.desc: On the second evening at Jotapata, answering Nathaniel's confusion about prayer, thanksgiving, and worship, Jesus taught the twenty-four about prayer at length. Harboring iniquity breaks the prayer connection; prayer changes man's attitude, not God; selfish prayer is to be avoided, and thanksgiving leads to worship.
acts.note.146:3.desc: At Ramah Jesus talked with an aged Greek philosopher who held that science and philosophy were enough, acknowledging the truth in his views before teaching him the gospel, and the man believed. He told Thomas that assurance of the kingdom rests on personal experience, its sign being love for one's fellows. At Zebulun he spoke of religion's social obligations.
acts.note.146:4.desc: At Iron Jesus spent most of his time working in the mines with the miners while the apostles preached from house to house. On the third afternoon he cleansed a leper, but when the man spread the news, Jesus had to leave town. They went on to Gischala, Chorazin, and Madon, but at Chorazin the message was almost wholly rejected, disheartening the apostles.
acts.note.146:4.diff: The Gospels place this healing simply in one of the cities, whereas The Urantia Book sets it at Iron, a mining town, on the third afternoon while Jesus was working with the miners.
acts.note.sub:146:4.3–5.desc: Late on the third afternoon at Iron, as Jesus returned from the mines, a leper knelt before him, saying he could make him clean if he would, and asking to enter the kingdom. Jesus touched him and said, be clean, and he was healed at once, but he disobeyed the charge to tell no one and, instead of going to the priest, spread the news through the town.
acts.note.sub:146:4.3–5.diff: The Gospels give this as one healing among many, whereas The Urantia Book states it was the first so-called miracle Jesus performed intentionally, and a case of real leprosy.
acts.note.146:5.desc: The apostles rejoiced when Jesus went to Cana. On the third day Titus, a prominent citizen of Capernaum, came begging him to heal his dying son, and Jesus said, "Return to your home; your son will live." When people then flocked to him seeking healing even from a distance, Jesus hurried away to Nain.
acts.note.146:5.diff: The Gospel of John ends this as Jesus' second sign after coming to Galilee, whereas The Urantia Book adds that the people of Cana then even sent messengers seeking healing at a distance, so Jesus hastened away.
acts.sub.146:5.2: The nobleman's son of Capernaum healed
acts.note.sub:146:5.2.desc: When Titus, a nobleman of Capernaum, begged Jesus at Cana to heal his son, Jesus lamented that they would not believe without signs and wonders, then after a moment's silent meditation told him to go home. On the way his servants met him with news that the fever had left the boy yesterday about the seventh hour, and Titus and his whole household believed.
acts.note.sub:146:5.2.diff: The Gospel of John records this as a sign, whereas The Urantia Book says it was not a miraculous healing but Jesus' foreknowledge of the working of natural law, and it names the nobleman Titus.
acts.note.146:6.desc: Leaving Cana for Nain, Jesus and his company met a funeral procession at the city gate for a widow's only son. Begged to help, Jesus perceived that the boy was not really dead, said, "Weep not. Your son is not dead; he sleeps," and took his hand and raised him. Though he explained, people believed the dead had been raised, and he left for Endor the next day.
acts.note.146:6.diff: The Gospel of Luke says Jesus raised the dead young man, whereas The Urantia Book says the boy was not really dead but deeply asleep, as Jesus explained, and that only Luke recorded the episode, as it was related to him.
acts.note.146:7.desc: At Endor Jesus rested a few days from the crowds seeking healing and retold the apostles the story of King Saul and the witch of Endor. He explained that the rebellious midwayers who impersonated spirits of the dead would soon be brought under control, and that departed human spirits do not return to communicate with the living.
acts.map24.head: The Passover Journey to Jerusalem
acts.map24.1.head: Two weeks at the Bethsaida headquarters
acts.map24.1.body: Arriving in Capernaum on Wednesday, March 17, A.D. 28, they spent two weeks there. Jesus, with James and John Zebedee, made two secret trips to Tiberias (dashed). On the day before they left, the servant of Mangus, the centurion, began to mend.
acts.map24.2.head: By the Jordan valley to Bethany
acts.map24.2.body: Early on Tuesday morning, March 30, they started for the Passover by the route of the Jordan valley. Resting at Jericho, Judas deposited some of their common funds in a bank; on Friday afternoon, April 2, they arrived at Bethany.
acts.map24.3.head: Bethany and Gethsemane
acts.map24.3.body: To avoid the crowds they pitched tents at Gethsemane, and the Master went back and forth from Bethany. Almost three weeks with no public preaching, only private teaching and personal work.
acts.map24.4.head: The pool of Bethesda
acts.map24.4.body: On the afternoon of the second Sabbath in Jerusalem, John led Jesus out through one of the city gates to the pool of Bethesda. A long-afflicted man picked up his bed and went forth to his home.
acts.map24.5.head: By Jericho to the Jordan ford
acts.map24.5.body: The last week of April they left the Bethany headquarters to return by way of Jericho and the Jordan. Peter preached to the multitude at the crossing of the Jordan.
acts.map24.6.head: Three days toward Amathus
acts.map24.6.body: The next morning they moved up the river toward Amathus and stayed three days, preaching, teaching, and baptizing. Leaving early Sabbath morning, May 1, they went only one thousand yards, a Sabbath day's journey. The route beyond is not in the text (dashed).
acts.map24.7.head: From Tarichea by boat to Bethsaida
acts.map24.7.body: Around noon on Monday, May 3, they came to Bethsaida by boat from Tarichea, to escape those who journeyed with them.
acts.note.147:0.desc: Jesus and the apostles returned to Capernaum on Wednesday, March 17, and spent two weeks at the Bethsaida headquarters before going to Jerusalem. The apostles taught by the seaside, while Jesus, with James and John, made two secret trips to Tiberias to teach believers, many of Herod's household, whose influence lessened Herod's enmity.
acts.note.147:1.desc: The day before they left for the Passover, Mangus, a Roman centurion at Capernaum, asked the synagogue elders to beg Jesus to heal his dying servant. As Jesus went, the centurion sent friends to say that a word would suffice, and Jesus said he had not found so great faith, not even in Israel. From that hour the servant began to mend.
acts.note.147:1.diff: The Gospel of Matthew has the centurion come in person and the servant healed at once, whereas The Urantia Book has him send elders and friends, names him Mangus, says the servant recovered gradually, and admits no one knew just what happened.
acts.note.147:2.desc: Early on Tuesday, March 30, the party set out for the Passover by way of the Jordan valley and reached Bethany on Friday afternoon, April 2. At Jericho Judas deposited part of the common funds in a bank. Jesus allowed no public preaching, only personal work, and at Bethany they quietly kept their first bloodless Passover.
acts.note.147:2.diff: The Gospel of John says only that Jesus went up to Jerusalem for a feast of the Jews, whereas The Urantia Book gives the dates and route and identifies the feast as the Passover.
acts.note.147:3.desc: On the afternoon of the second Sabbath in Jerusalem, John led Jesus out of the city to the pool of Bethesda, hoping for a miracle. Jesus declined and spoke words of comfort and eternal life to the sufferers as children of God. A man long afflicted by a troubled mind rejoiced, took up his bed, and went home.
acts.note.147:3.diff: The Gospel of John says an angel stirred the water and Jesus commanded a man ill thirty-eight years to rise and walk, whereas The Urantia Book calls the pool a hot spring bubbling from gas, and the man took up his bed himself, heartened by Jesus' words.
acts.note.147:4.desc: That same Sabbath evening, in Lazarus's garden at Bethany, Nathaniel asked how to apply the golden rule to evil people. Jesus taught six levels of interpreting this rule of living: the flesh, the feelings, the mind, brotherly love, the moral, and the spiritual. The highest is to treat others as God would treat them.
acts.note.147:5.desc: Simon, an influential Pharisee of Jerusalem, invited Jesus with Peter, James, and John to a meal. A woman who had closed her brothel and believed the gospel came in, wet Jesus' feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them. Jesus answered Simon's unspoken thoughts with a parable of forgiven debts and said her sins were forgiven.
acts.note.147:5.diff: The Gospel of Luke calls her simply a sinner of the city, whereas The Urantia Book says she had already believed and closed her brothel, and adds Jesus' words about Simon's inner conflict and that evening's address on the direction of progress.
acts.note.147:6.desc: In the last week of April Jesus and the twelve set out for Capernaum, while the Sanhedrin sent six secret spies after them. After three days of teaching near Amathus, they left on the Sabbath morning, May 1, Jesus limiting the march to a Sabbath day's journey; but when the apostles rubbed grain in a wheat field, the spies found fault.
acts.note.147:6.diff: The Gospels say only that Pharisees objected to the incident in the grainfields, whereas The Urantia Book identifies them as six spies sent by the Sanhedrin and says Jesus kept to a Sabbath day's journey from the start.
acts.sub.147:6.4–5: The apostles pluck grain on the Sabbath
acts.note.sub:147:6.4–5.desc: On a narrow road through the wheat, hungry apostles plucked grain, and the spies first challenged Andrew for rubbing it in his hands. When they protested to Jesus, he cited David's eating the showbread and said the Sabbath was made for man and the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath. The Pharisees dared not ask more.
acts.note.sub:147:6.4–5.diff: The Gospels have the Pharisees go straight to Jesus and include the example of the priests in the temple, whereas The Urantia Book first records an argument with Andrew and adds Jesus' words about caring for his associates' welfare.
acts.note.147:7.desc: Around noon on Monday, May 3, Jesus and the twelve came by boat from Tarichea to Bethsaida to escape the crowds following them, but by the next day many, including the spies from Jerusalem, had found him again. At Tuesday evening's question hour, the leader of the spies asked about fasting.
acts.note.147:7.diff: The Gospels do not fix the time or place of this exchange, whereas The Urantia Book places it in early May after the return to Bethsaida, with a Jerusalem spy asking the question.
acts.sub.147:7.2–3: The question about fasting; old teachings and new
acts.note.sub:147:7.2–3.desc: When the leader of the spies asked why Jesus never had his disciples fast and pray, Jesus, referring to a statement by John, said the sons of the bridechamber do not fast while the bridegroom is with them, and spoke of new cloth on old garments and new wine in old skins. What is old and also true must abide; what is new but false must be rejected.
acts.note.sub:147:7.2–3.diff: The Gospels say John's disciples asked, whereas The Urantia Book has the leader of the spies ask, and adds that fasting is not part of the gospel of the kingdom and that what is old and true must abide.
acts.note.147:8.desc: That night, after the listeners had gone, Jesus taught the apostles until after two in the morning, beginning with Isaiah's words on fasting. True fasting is to free the oppressed and share bread with the hungry, and it is their faith, not fasting of the flesh, that makes them secure in the kingdom.
acts.map25.head: The Zebedee Camp and the Second Preaching Tour of Galilee
acts.map25.1.head: The Zebedee home and the seaside camp
acts.map25.1.body: From May 3 to October 3, A.D. 28, Jesus and the apostles were in residence at the Zebedee home at Bethsaida. The tented city by the seaside numbered from five hundred to fifteen hundred; the school of evangelists met there, and a short distance to the south of the camp stood Elman's infirmary.
acts.map25.2.head: The second public preaching tour of Galilee
acts.map25.2.body: From Sunday, October 3, to December 30. The twelve apostles and the newly recruited corps of 117 evangelists worked in groups, while Jesus, with James and John, often visited two cities in one day to encourage them. Squares mark the cities the text names; it gives no order or route.
acts.map25.3.head: Gathering at the Zebedee home
acts.map25.3.body: David Zebedee kept the headquarters at Bethsaida and sent out messengers. By supper time on rainy Thursday, December 30, all the apostles and evangelists had arrived at the Zebedee home.
acts.note.148:0.desc: From May 3 to October 3, A.D. 28, Jesus and the apostles resided at the Zebedee home in Bethsaida. By the seaside a tented encampment housing five hundred to fifteen hundred people was run under the management of David Zebedee, while Peter was in full charge of the school of the evangelists.
acts.note.148:1.desc: Peter, James, and Andrew screened applicants for the school of evangelists, and the students taught the people by the seaside in the afternoon what they had learned in the morning. Each apostle taught his own view of the gospel, and the hundred and more evangelists trained there later furnished the material for choosing the seventy.
acts.note.148:2.desc: Elman, the Syrian physician, assisted by twenty-five young women and twelve men, conducted for four months the kingdom's first hospital. Jesus visited the sick at least three times a week, yet among the thousand who recovered there, not one supernatural miracle was performed.
acts.note.148:3.desc: During this period Jesus often went into the hills with only two apostles and remained much alone, saying he was "about the Father's business." The recorders infer that in these solitary seasons he was directing many of his chief directors of universe affairs.
acts.note.148:4.desc: In a private talk in the Zebedee garden, Thomas asked about evil, and Jesus distinguished evil, sin, and iniquity by the degree of transgression of the Father's will. He taught that man is not a fallen being but one ascending to God, and that exposure to evil does not make one a sinner.
acts.note.148:5.desc: When Nathaniel asked why the Father allows his children to suffer, Jesus explained that rebellious traitors had upset the natural order of this world. The Father does not purposely afflict his children, he taught, and much affliction is produced by sin and iniquity.
acts.note.148:6.desc: That same evening John asked why innocent people suffer, and Jesus expounded the story of Job, pointing out the mistaken ideas of God held by his three friends. Human suffering is not a visitation of divine judgment, he said, and Job by faith found a God of comfort and salvation.
acts.note.148:7.desc: On the second Sabbath before the second preaching tour, Jesus spoke in the Capernaum synagogue and then healed a man with a withered hand whom the leader of the Pharisaic spies had sent to him. This was his first miracle in response to his enemies' challenge; the Pharisees went to Herod at Tiberias, but Herod refused to act.
acts.note.148:7.diff: The Gospels say the Pharisees took counsel to destroy Jesus, whereas The Urantia Book adds that the spies' leader induced the man to come, that Herod refused to act, and that the man was a stone mason.
acts.note.148:8.desc: In the last week at Bethsaida, Abraham, a young member of the Sanhedrin, was baptized by Abner, stirring up Jerusalem. Kirmeth, a trance prophet from Bagdad, disturbed the camp, and Abraham gave all his worldly goods to the apostolic treasury, helping to send forth the evangelists.
acts.note.148:9.desc: On Friday afternoon, October 1, during a meeting in the front room of the Zebedee home, a paralytic from Capernaum was let down by his friends through the roof tiles with ropes. Jesus declared his sins forgiven and bade him rise and walk, and three of the spies believed and were baptized by Peter.
acts.note.148:9.diff: The Gospels place this in a house at Capernaum (Matthew, "his own city"), whereas The Urantia Book sets it at the Zebedee home in Bethsaida and adds that three Jerusalem spies were afterward baptized.
acts.note.149:0.desc: The second public preaching tour of Galilee began on Sunday, October 3, A.D. 28, and ended on December 30. Jesus took only James and John with him and oversaw the 117 new evangelists, while David Zebedee kept the headquarters of his messenger service at Bethsaida.
acts.note.149:1.desc: By the time the Bethsaida camp broke up, Jesus' fame as a healer had spread throughout Palestine and Syria. On this tour he deliberately performed no miracles, yet more than a hundred people were healed unconsciously, which the recorders attribute to faith, his compassion, and the Father's will working together.
acts.note.149:1.diff: The Gospels say Jesus healed all the sick, whereas The Urantia Book explains that on this tour he did not intentionally heal, and the healings occurred through faith without Jesus being conscious of them.
acts.note.149:2.desc: The recorder notes how Jesus' teachings were later overlaid by the doctrine of the atonement and a theology centered on his person. Jesus was free from superstition, appointed women as teachers of the gospel, and as a progressive evolutionist rather than a militant revolutionist won people's confidence and love.
acts.note.149:3.desc: The common people welcomed Jesus, but the religious leaders at Jerusalem grew more hostile after the conversion of Abraham and the desertion of the three spies. The Pharisees had a systematic theology while Jesus taught by parables, and from this time the leaders never ceased plotting his death.
acts.note.149:4.desc: On the tour Jesus held evening classes with believers in many towns. When a young evangelist asked about anger, he called it a sign that the spiritual nature has failed to control mind and body, and he taught balanced character, showing that virtues carried to extremes become vices.
acts.note.149:5.desc: At an evening conference of the evangelists under Simon Zelotes, Simon asked about contentment. Jesus taught that happiness depends very much on one's willingness to be led by the indwelling spirit, and urged them to seek the assurance of faith and the sureties of divine sonship.
acts.note.149:6.desc: At an evening conference at Gamala, Philip asked how to harmonize the Scripture's call to fear the Lord with Jesus' teaching. Jesus said men must advance from fear through reverence to love, adoring God not as a mighty king to be feared but as a merciful Father.
acts.note.149:7.desc: At Andrew's direction all the preaching groups returned to the Zebedee home at Bethsaida by Thursday, December 30. The party was granted a two weeks' recess, and of the 117 evangelists only about seventy-five survived the test of experience and were ready to continue in service.
acts.intro.150: Setting out on the third preaching tour
acts.map26.head: The Third Preaching Tour and the Visit to Nazareth
acts.map26.1.head: From Bethsaida on the third preaching tour
acts.map26.1.body: On Tuesday, January 18, A.D. 29, the tested evangelists joined the twenty-four at the Zebedee house to prepare for a mission of seven weeks. They visited Magdala, Tiberias, Nazareth, and the cities and villages of central and southern Galilee. At Magdala the women evangelists first demonstrated their usefulness.
acts.map26.2.head: By Shunem to Nazareth
acts.map26.2.body: One evening at Shunem, after John's apostles had returned to Hebron, Jesus taught. All were to assemble at Nazareth on Friday, March 4 (the order and route of the stops are not in the text; dashed).
acts.map26.3.head: Rejected at Nazareth, back to Bethsaida
acts.map26.3.body: On the Sabbath he spoke in the Nazareth synagogue and was rejected. Leaving Sunday morning by different routes, they all assembled at Bethsaida by noon on Thursday, March 10.
acts.map26.4.head: Across the lake to Kheresa
acts.map26.4.body: Crossing on Sunday evening, they met a sudden windstorm. The next morning, near the cemetery of the village of Kheresa, Amos the lunatic was cured.
acts.map26.5.head: Back to Bethsaida
acts.map26.5.body: After only one night of rest, early Tuesday morning the swine-raising gentiles urged them to depart. Landing that Tuesday forenoon, Jesus aroused the daughter of Jairus.
acts.note.150:0.desc: In January, A.D. 29, Abner and the apostles of John held a joint conference with Jesus' apostles at Bethsaida, but Jesus declined to take part in the discussion of anointing the sick. On Tuesday, January 18, the twenty-four joined about seventy-five evangelists for the seven-week third preaching tour of Galilee.
acts.note.150:0.diff: The Gospels say only that Jesus went about all the cities and villages, whereas The Urantia Book details that the evangelists went out in groups of five and that Abner's associates worked with them for almost three weeks.
acts.note.150:1.desc: On the evening of January 16 Jesus announced that ten women would be set apart for the ministering work of the kingdom. The ten, including Susanna, Joanna the wife of Chuza, Martha, and Rachel, were appointed and elected Susanna their chief and Joanna their treasurer; Mary Magdalene and Rebecca were added later.
acts.note.150:1.diff: The Gospel of Luke says only that women ministered to Jesus of their substance, whereas The Urantia Book says Jesus formally set apart ten women as gospel teachers and names all ten and their organization.
acts.note.150:2.desc: The women's corps first proved its usefulness at Magdala, entering places of evil where the apostles could hardly go. Through the work of Martha and Rachel, Mary Magdalene, then in a house of ill repute, believed and was baptized by Peter, and about four weeks later she was set apart at Jotapata.
acts.note.150:3.desc: At Tiberias the women conducted the apostolic party's Sabbath service, Joanna leading it in the banquet room of Herod's new palace. That evening, answering Andrew's question about a new star, Jesus rejected every superstition, including astrology, charms, divination, dream interpretation, and idols.
acts.note.150:4.desc: The next evening Jesus said the harvest was plenteous but the laborers few, and he sent the twelve out two and two throughout Galilee. They were not to go to gentile cities or Samaria but to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, and they would meet again at Nazareth.
acts.note.150:4.diff: The Gospels say Jesus gave power to cast out unclean spirits and heal, with instructions about what to carry, whereas The Urantia Book has no such grant of power or instructions and lists the pairs of apostles.
acts.note.sub:150:4.3.desc: Jesus encouraged them that not even two sparrows are forgotten by God and that the hairs of their heads are numbered, so they need not fear. Since rejection of the gospel would divide households, they should strive to save whole families, yet whoever loves parents more than the gospel is not worthy of the kingdom.
acts.note.sub:150:4.3.diff: Matthew says Jesus came to bring not peace but a sword, whereas The Urantia Book says he came to bring peace, that division follows when it is rejected, and urges saving the whole family.
acts.note.150:5.desc: At Shunem, Rachel asked how to answer women who ask what they must do to be saved, and Jesus said: believe the gospel and accept divine forgiveness. Salvation is the gift of God, he taught, and righteous living is the fruit of the spirit-born life of sonship.
acts.note.150:6.desc: For the rest of the tour Jesus moved among the groups, speaking each evening on subjects such as the love of God, dreams and visions, and humility and meekness. All the groups assembled on Friday, March 4, at an encampment in the highlands north of Nazareth.
acts.note.150:7.desc: On Friday afternoon, March 4, Jesus walked about Nazareth wholly unrecognized, passing his childhood home, the carpenter shop, the hill, and the synagogue. The people of Nazareth resented that he had done no great works in his home town, and his enemies had hired rough men to stir up trouble at the Sabbath service.
acts.note.150:8.desc: On the Sabbath morning the Nazareth synagogue service was conducted in the old way, and Jesus read from Deuteronomy and Isaiah out of the scroll he himself had once presented. He declared, "Today are these Scriptures fulfilled," spoke for almost fifteen minutes on the sons and daughters of God, then stepped down into the questioning crowd.
acts.note.150:8.diff: The Gospel of Luke says Jesus read only from Isaiah, whereas The Urantia Book says he first read from Deuteronomy, spoke on the sons and daughters of God, and that hired men sought to cause a disturbance.
acts.note.150:9.desc: When his enemies mocked him, Jesus replied that a prophet is without honor in his own country. Simon Zelotes' militant blunder inflamed the mob, which tried to push Jesus over a cliff, but when he turned and faced them with folded arms, the crowd parted. The party reassembled at Bethsaida on March 10.
acts.note.150:9.diff: The Gospel of Luke says the crowd was enraged by the stories of Elijah and Elisha, whereas The Urantia Book omits these stories and says Simon Zelotes' blunder and the hired men stirred up the riot.
acts.note.151:0.desc: By March 10 all the preaching groups had gathered at Bethsaida, and Jesus spent most of the Sabbath alone in the hills. That Saturday night he spoke for more than an hour on the mission of adversity and the spiritual value of disappointment, still sorrowing over his rejection at Nazareth.
acts.note.151:1.desc: One Sunday morning, seated in an old fishing boat by the seaside, Jesus for the first time used parables, telling a crowd of about a thousand the story of the sower. That evening Matthew asked why he spoke in parables, and Jesus answered that those who desire truth would understand while his enemies would be confounded.
acts.note.151:1.diff: The Gospels report only the teaching from a boat by the sea, whereas The Urantia Book says this was when Jesus first began the parable method and that Matthew asked his question that evening in the Zebedee garden.
acts.note.151:2.desc: Peter and Nathaniel interpreted the parable of the sower differently, assigning spiritual meanings to each detail, and the apostles split into two camps. Thomas said a parable teaches one great truth, here that the results of ministry vary with conditions, and Jesus acknowledged that Thomas had discerned its true meaning.
acts.note.151:2.diff: In the Gospels Jesus himself interprets the parable detail by detail, whereas in The Urantia Book that interpretation is Peter's; Jesus warns against turning parables into allegories and approves Thomas's view.
acts.note.151:3.desc: The next evening Jesus taught them to suit their teaching to their hearers, speaking of setting a lamp on a lampstand, and explained how parables plant truth while avoiding prejudice. At the close he added, as the last of the parable of the sower, the story of seed that grows of itself until the harvest.
acts.note.151:3.diff: In the Gospels the sayings about the lamp and hidden things follow directly after the parable's interpretation, whereas The Urantia Book places them in the next evening's class on the value of parables.
acts.note.151:4.desc: The next day Jesus again taught the multitude from the boat, giving the parables of the wheat and the weeds, the mustard seed, the leaven, the treasure hidden in a field, the pearl of great price, and the sweep net. From then on he taught the masses almost only by parables, expounding them more fully to the apostles and evangelists in the evening classes.
acts.note.151:4.diff: Matthew interprets the parables of the weeds and the net as judgment at the end of the world, whereas The Urantia Book gives no such interpretation and presents only the parables.
acts.note.151:5.desc: Weary of the throngs, Jesus set out across the lake with his apostles on Sunday afternoon, and at evening a sudden gale filled the boat with water, so Peter woke him. As Jesus said, "Peace, be quiet," the storm subsided, which the recorders regard as a coincidence.
acts.note.151:5.diff: The Gospels say Jesus rebuked the wind and the sea and calmed them, whereas The Urantia Book says he spoke to the apostles' troubled minds and the storm's ending was a coincidence.
acts.note.151:6.desc: Amos, a lunatic living in the tomb caverns near Kheresa, fell at Jesus' feet, and Jesus told him he was not possessed of a devil and commanded him to come out of his spell, restoring his mind. Meanwhile dogs drove a herd of swine over a precipice, giving rise to the legend that the devils entered the swine, and the villagers asked Jesus to leave.
acts.note.151:6.diff: The Gospels say the demons entered the swine and the herd perished, whereas The Urantia Book says dogs merely drove about thirty swine and Amos had a mental affliction, not possession. Matthew speaks of two men.
